answers.answer: SCOPe 2.08 does not reclassify the fragment structures to a different fold. In the release-scoped records I queried (release 2.08, the current release per the API), 1br0 chain A, 1ez3 chains A, B and C, and 1dn1 chain B all carry the same domain classification, a.47.2.1 (class a, all-alpha; fold a.47; superfamily a.47.2; family a.47.2.1). The fragment-based assignments therefore agree with the full-domain assignment in 1dn1 B. Read them as independent support for one family, not as evidence that fragments define a separate fold. Three interpretive points follow. (1) Family assignment depends on the domain's structural core, so a fragment that retains that core can carry the label, but the fragment does not establish domain boundaries or termini. Boundaries should come from the full domain (1dn1 B or 3c98 B). The API returned no residue ranges for the 1br0 or 1ez3 domains, so I could not confirm from these records that they are truncated relative to 1dn1 B. (2) 1dn1 is obsolete in this release (obsolete 2008-03-25, obsoleted by 3c98, 'Revised structure of the munc18a-syntaxin1 complex'). Use 3c98 as the representative entry. Its chain B is also a.47.2.1, and its chain A is e.25.1.1, matching 1dn1 chain A, so the partner classification is stable across the revision. (3) 1ez3's three chains are three separately classified domains of the same family, not three families. Limits: concordant family classification reflects structural similarity of the classified domains. It does not transfer function (for example SNARE-motif binding or autoinhibition) from a fragment to the full protein. Because the N-terminal domain's conformation can depend on its binding partner, a fragment's conformation should not be used as a template for the bound state without experimental evidence for the full domain or complex. Function claims should rest on experimental data, not on the fold label alone.
